newsitem.title: USA: No tradeoff between inflation and growth--SF Fed.
newsitem.headline: No tradeoff between inflation and growth--SF Fed.

text.p: A central bank should not allow a pick-up in inflation in a bid to boost the economy in the short run because the gains in output would prove to be only temporary, the head of the San Francisco Fed said Friday.

"Both empirical and theoretical research indicate that in the long run there is no tradeoff between the rate of inflation and growth," San Francisco Fed president Robert Parry told an audience of economists here.
"In other words, any gains in employment or output are only temporary," the San Francisco Fed chief added.
Parry said the main goal of central banks when setting their monetary policy should be the maintenance of a low inflation scenario.
He added that the best contribution a central bank could provide to economic growth was an environment in which price rises were subdued and monetary policy was credible.
"The main thing monetary policy can do is control inflation," Parry said.
So how does a central bank conduct low-inflation policy?
"For the U.S. and many other industrialized countries a good deal of emphasis has been placed on the importance of making such (monetary) policies credible," Parry said.
Parry explained that "easy" monetary policy could provide a boost to the economy in the short run, adding that such a phenomenon could make it tempting for central banks to "go for the quick fix."

But that formula, he said, would just tend to fuel inflation in the long run. "A central bank simply doesn't have the power to push an economy beyond its capacity to produce goods and services for very long," Parry said.
He also said that over the last two years China had managed to achieve solid economic growth and a steep decline in inflation rates.

He said, however, there was "still much to do, and the path ahead will be difficult. But I trust that these successes will provide the stimulus for keeping the process of financial reform ... moving in the right direction."

The San Francisco Fed president spoke to the Chinese Economists Society at the University of Southern California here. The speech did not include any further comments on the current economic scenario in the United States.
